Giá vàng thế giới hôm nay 8/8/2026
Lúc 21h ngày 7/8 (giờ Việt Nam), giá vàng giao ngay giao dịch ở mức 4.354 USD/ounce, tăng 114 USD. Giá vàng kỳ hạn giao tháng 10/2026 giao dịch ở mức 4.395 USD/ounce.
Theo Cục Thống kê Lao động Mỹ (BLS), số việc làm phi nông nghiệp của Mỹ giảm 23.000 việc làm trong tháng 7, trong khi các chuyên gia kinh tế dự báo tăng khoảng 85.000 việc làm. Đây là lần thứ hai số việc làm phi nông nghiệp giảm trong năm nay.
Trong khi đó, số liệu do Bộ Lao động Mỹ công bố ngày 6/8 cho thấy, số đơn xin trợ cấp thất nghiệp lần đầu tăng 1.000 đơn, lên 199.000 đơn trong tuần kết thúc ngày 1/8, sau khi điều chỉnh theo yếu tố mùa vụ. Số liệu của tuần trước cũng được điều chỉnh tăng 1.000 đơn, lên 198.000 đơn.
Đây là tuần thứ ba liên tiếp số đơn xin trợ cấp thất nghiệp lần đầu duy trì dưới 200.000 đơn, đánh dấu chuỗi dài nhất kể từ tháng 3/2023.
Dữ liệu việc làm yếu hơn kỳ vọng khiến thị trường giảm bớt kỳ vọng Fed sẽ tiếp tục thắt chặt chính sách tiền tệ. Theo giới phân tích, nhà đầu tư vàng đang kỳ vọng Cục Dự trữ Liên bang Mỹ (Fed) sẽ khó có khả năng tiếp tục tăng lãi suất trong năm nay, ngay cả khi áp lực lạm phát vẫn dai dẳng, qua đó hạn chế đà tăng của lợi suất thực và hỗ trợ giá vàng.
Thị trường trái phiếu vẫn đang phản ánh khả năng Fed tăng lãi suất trong tháng 9. Theo công cụ FedWatch của CME, thị trường hiện đánh giá xác suất Fed tăng lãi suất trong cuộc họp tháng 9 ở mức khoảng 50/50.
Dự báo giá vàng
Triển vọng giá vàng đang dần cải thiện khi những yếu tố từng gây sức ép lên kim loại quý có dấu hiệu suy yếu. Lợi suất thực của Mỹ được cho là đã tiến gần đỉnh, đồng USD có thể chuyển từ yếu tố cản trở sang hỗ trợ giá vàng.
Theo giới phân tích, vàng không nhất thiết phải chờ Fed giảm lãi suất mới có thể tăng trở lại. Chỉ cần lợi suất thực không tiếp tục tăng, chi phí cơ hội nắm giữ vàng sẽ giảm, tạo dư địa cho giá phục hồi.
Bên cạnh đó, nhu cầu mua vàng của các ngân hàng trung ương, xu hướng đa dạng hóa dự trữ và phi đô la hóa tiếp tục tạo nền tảng hỗ trợ dài hạn.
Trong ngắn hạn, giá vàng có thể vẫn biến động do triển vọng lãi suất và diễn biến giá dầu. Tuy nhiên, nếu giữ vững vùng 4.000 USD/ounce, kim loại quý có cơ hội hình thành đáy và hướng trở lại xu hướng tăng.
Trong một báo cáo công bố tuần trước, ông Christopher Wood, Giám đốc chiến lược cổ phiếu toàn cầu tại Jefferies, cảnh báo rằng nếu làn sóng đầu tư vốn vào trí tuệ nhân tạo (AI) hiện nay sụp đổ, Cục Dự trữ Liên bang Mỹ (Fed) sẽ không còn nhiều dư địa để tăng lãi suất.
Theo ông, đây là thời điểm nhà đầu tư có thể bắt đầu tích lũy trở lại vàng và cổ phiếu khai thác vàng sau một thời gian dài tạm dừng. Ông cho rằng xu hướng đặt cược vào khả năng đồng USD suy yếu do mất giá chỉ đang tạm thời lắng xuống, nhưng chưa biến mất.

articles.title: Musician and entrepreneur Tom Vek is building a digital music player, but don’t call it retro
articles.text:
Tom Vek burst onto the scene in 2005 with his album We Have Sound, which garnered a solid 7.6 from the tastemakers of the day over at Pitchfork. His undeniably catchy brand of dancy indietronica landed him an appearance on The OC and placement on the Grand Theft Auto IV soundtrack. His follow-up, Leisure Seizure, had a lengthy gestation period, but arrived in 2011 to similar success, reaching No. 79 on the UK charts.
Musician and entrepreneur Tom Vek is building a digital music player, but don’t call it retro
The Sleevenote creator is ready for the offline resurgence, but wants to move on from CDs and cassettes.
Musician and entrepreneur Tom Vek is building a digital music player, but don’t call it retro
The Sleevenote creator is ready for the offline resurgence, but wants to move on from CDs and cassettes.
Vek has continued to release music at regular intervals over the last 15 years, dropping Newer Symbols in 2022. But in 2020 he started toying with this idea he had for a music player called Sleevenote. Inspired by vinyl packaging, it was his way of trying to bring some of the beauty and magic of cover art and liner notes to your digital audio. Securing parts, like square screens, proved difficult. Plus, the original prototype was enormous — roughly the size of a 7-inch single, just thicker and heavier.
Now Vek is back with a new version of Sleevenote that’s smaller, cheaper, and, for a little while longer, available to purchase. The last handful of the Day One Editions are available now for $349. As he turns his attention to the next chapter for his media player passion project, he told us about the essentials, his obsessions, and pet peeves as a musician-turned-entrepreneur.
What is your most indispensable tool (analog or digital, app or hardware)?
As much as I’d love to say my GMT wristwatch, because of all the communication we do with our friends in Seattle, and my love of wristwatches, the real answer has to be a MacBook. I’m either designing UI, designing graphics, retouching photos, or making videos, discussing ideas, implementing ideas, or hearing how my ideas go down. It truly is the motorbike for my mind. I have to see ideas to know whether I like them or not. I’m very fickle regarding industrial design of the tech I use and a big fan of the current “M” MacBooks, Apple kinda lost it for a bit.
How many tabs do you have open right now?
I get a lot of shit from Sleevenote co-founder Chris for how many tabs I have open, also in multiple Chrome profiles, you know, to the point the tabs get so narrow that you have to remember what it is from the favicon. I like coming back to things, as well as having a selection of regularly used things in a row. I find it useful for remembering all the social apps I’m meant to be posting my latest Sleevenote graphic to.
Which tech trend do you wish would go away?
This is a bit salty, but the trend for new retro-style CD players and cassette players. It is a great sign that people want offline dedicated music experiences, but I want to see new ideas. I’m specifically interested in ideas that push for digital music purchasing because it’s far better for musicians than buying that second-hand CD. I want my kids’ generation not to be stuck in a retro cycle, or a doomed big tech cycle. I want to see thoughtfully created indie tech products that could not have existed at any other time. Plus, I remember cassettes, they sound awful.
What is one thing you wish you had created?
I will answer this with a song: three years after my debut album, when I should have had my second album together, I heard “Jump In The Pool” by Friendly Fires, featuring one of the most stunning synth solos of all time. I would have loved to have created that song at that time. Especially since I’d pushed myself and my then manager fully-clothed into a pool around that time and hadn’t even thought to write a song about it.
What is your current obsession?
Been an obsession for quite a while but it’s still: carports in architecture. I’m a car guy, I’m a very visually-focused car guy. I’m not really fussed about performance or track racing or anything. My real love is the design of the automobile and how it’s an emotive expression of movement. The perfect abode to me has car(s) on show, not hidden away in a garage, but still protected, so the carport becomes this perfect idea. I’m obsessed with mid-century desert architecture which incorporated the automobile so well into the language of the house, but even in the rainy UK, being able to get in and out of your car without getting wet would just make me so happy, I think haha.
What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?
I buy lots of fiction books. I love a small paperback. I just picked up a book called The Cowards based purely on the cover. I’ve just finished a load of Steinbeck, so looking for something else. It’s funny that I often use the shortest elevator pitch “Sleevenote is a Kindle for music”, but I’ve never liked the idea of a digital book. Most people read one book at a time, but having all your music accessible at any one time is much more of a reason for a digitisation of a collection, it seems to me.
What do you think is worth splurging on?
Digital music downloads are worth splurging on. We’ve been led to believe there’s no point in buying anything digitally, but it’s standing in plain sight as the best thing to do with things like music. Not only does it send far greater support for artists, but it gives us music fans offline and time-stamped access to great art, and being encouraged to spend some time with a curated selection of art, we all know is good for the mind and soul. I want Sleevenote to enable this.
What would the tagline for your biopic be?
Encompassing all my work, I suspect it would be “Nothing But Green Lights”, the name of one of my songs, which I’d also apply to my work with other projects. It’s good, not always easy, to try to think there’s nothing in the way of going where you want to go.
What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

articles.title: Your phone's USB-C port does a lot more than just charge - Here's what else it can do - Engadget
articles.text:
Your phone's USB-C port does a lot more than just charge - Here's what else it can do
You might be surprised at how versatile it really is.
For a rocky couple of years in the 2010s, smartphone ports were a bit of a free-for-all. Apple was off doing one thing with Lightning, while Android devices were off doing another. The classic 3.5 mm headphone jacks disappeared, to the initial dismay of many audiophiles and anyone annoyed by the need to buy yet another cable adapter.
It took some time, but mobile devices have finally reached an accord. No matter the manufacturer, it's a pretty safe bet that any smartphones made during this decade will be fitted with a USB-C port.
USB-C has become a convenient catch-all that offers more consistency across device types. While this approach does have a handful of downsides, the main benefit is being able to use one universal connector in some creative and convenient new ways. A USB-C port is obviously your path to wired charging, but that's just the start of its potential.
Charging other devices
Most of us think of charging our phones by connecting them to a laptop, but the power dynamic can go the other way too. A smartphone can give some extra juice to another phone, wireless headphones or a smart watch via USB-C. All you need is a cable with USB-C connections at both ends.
Flash drives and memory card readers
If you have sensitive documents you don't want to risk transferring by email or by cloud, a flash drive is the best solution. In past years, these portable drives only offered USB-A, but that has happily changed with the times. For maximum access across devices, consider a device that has both USB-C and USB-A extendable ports.
In a similar vein, a smartphone can also be equipped with a portable memory card reader. This is particularly useful for anyone regularly working with very large files, such as photographers or videographers. Again, if flexibility is your goal, there are models on the market that have USB-A as well as USB-C port options. Depending on your most common activities, look for a device that can read and write both SD and microSD cards.
Typing on the go
Laptops are plenty portable, but sometimes you might want the flexibility to turn your smartphone into a petite workstation. USB-C can be used to connect many wired keyboard models for more efficient typing. It's great to have this option in case you don't want to compose an important work email entirely with your thumbs.
Connecting external displays
As bulky as they may be, even the phablet-sized phones only have so much screen real estate. Connect your device to an external monitor or a television with a USB-C for a better view. It's nice to have this wired approach as an alternative to the battery-intensive task of screen mirroring or casting. Use a dedicated USB-C to HDMI adapter if you only want to link up to a monitor, or hook up an entire smorgasbord of options by looking for a hub that offers as many as eight different ports.
Audio recording
Many content creators run their entire operation from a phone. Having high-quality audio in a video is a must, and there are a bunch of easy-to-use microphone options that will work well depending on where you're recording. If you want to step up mobile audio recording, there are microphones for any purpose and price point that can improve the quality of the final result.
Headphones
Whether it's a pair of "beater" headphones to use for heavy physical activity or a set intended for enjoying lossless audio, there might be times when wireless headphones don't fit the vibe. If wired is what you want, you may find newer models, like these two from Sennheiser, that come with USB-C cables to reflect the current standard for hardware ports. If your set is really old school, however, you may need an adapter so that the USB-C can link up with a 3.5mm audio cable. Fortunately, those are cheap and available from many different brands.
Gaming
Improve the ergonomics of your mobile gaming with USB-C. One way to do this is to simply connect a game controller. Playing with a wired connection is usually a better experience than over Bluetooth if you want to have fewer latency issues. Both Apple and Android devices can be synced up with most gaming brand hardware, including PlayStation and Xbox controllers.
Another way to level up your phone as a gaming station is by turning it into a handheld. Mobile gaming controllers, such as the Backbone One or Razer Kishi, take your thumbs off the screen and create an experience more like that of the Steam Deck or Nintendo Switch.
Powering scientific gadgets
These may not apply to the average person, but there are some impressively powerful tools that can be hooked up to a smartphone. While these phone-coupled options may not always be as powerful as their traditional counterparts, sometimes being able to take technical gear on the go is what's most important. Skilled tradespeople like plumbers and mechanics might appreciate having an endoscope camera in their kit for making quick assessments. Ultrasound devices that can be powered by a smartphone make it possible for medical workers to aid patients even in remote locations with limited equipment access.

articles.title: Is this $450 laptop from an unknown brand too good to be true?
articles.text:
Finding a good laptop under $500 was hard enough before RAMageddon. They nearly always had cheap hardware and underpowered, often outdated chips. That’s what made the MacBook Neo so disruptive: It offered great build quality and good-enough performance starting at $599. Windows laptops couldn’t touch it. Even though it’s gone up to $699, it’s still the laptop to beat.
Is this $450 laptop from an unknown brand too good to be true?
The Chuwi Unibook is meant to undercut the MacBook Neo, but you get what you pay for.
If you buy something from a Verge link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
So when little-known Chinese brand Chuwi announced a $450 Windows laptop with an aluminum build and a brand-new Intel Wildcat Lake processor, it sounded too good to be true.
It is.
Chuwi UniBook
The Good
- It’s $450
- Tons of ports for a small laptop (though none are very fast)
- Good battery life
The Bad
- A bad screen and absolutely awful trackpad, speakers, and webcam
- Metal chassis feels cheap, with lots of flex
- Lackluster performance from the Intel chip and limited RAM
- Concerns over long-term customer support
The UniBook comes in one configuration: a 14-inch with an Intel Core 3 304 processor, 8GB of soldered RAM, and a user-swappable 256GB SSD. That’s the lowest-end of Intel’s new Wildcat Lake chips, with just five CPU cores: one performance core, and four low-power efficiency cores. And the integrated graphics? A single GPU core. The MacBook Neo’s A18 Pro is a six-core CPU / five-core GPU ensemble, and it’s a hot rod by comparison.
Component report card
- Screen: D
- Webcam: D
- Keyboard: C
- Trackpad: F
- Port selection: A
- Speakers: F
- Number of ugly stickers to remove: 1
The UniBook feels sluggish in anything beyond basic web browsing, emails, and messaging. Its benchmark scores confirm how woefully underpowered that chip is. The MacBook Neo trounces it across the board: both single and multicore CPU performance, as well as graphics. Our Adobe Premiere 4K export test took over an hour on the UniBook. (Although at least it didn’t crash out.) I know it isn’t designed for video editing, but neither is the MacBook Neo, and the Neo exports the same video in under 10 minutes. The one edge the UniBook has is a slightly faster SSD.
|  | Chuwi UniBook / Intel Core 3 304 “Wildcat Lake” / 8GB / 256GB | MacBook Neo / Apple A18 Pro / 8GB / 256GB | Microsoft Surface Laptop 13-inch (2026) / Qualcomm Snapdragon X Plus X1P-46-100 / 8GB / 256GB | Acer Aspire 14 AI / Intel Core Ultra 7 256V “Lunar Lake” / 16GB / 1TB | Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3x / Qualcomm Snapdragon X X1-26-100 / 16GB / 256GB | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CPU cores | 5 | 6 | 8 | 8 | 8 | 
| GPU | Intel Graphics (1 GPU core) | A18 Pro (5 GPU cores) | Adreno X1-45 | Intel Arc 140V (8 GPU cores) | Adreno X1-26 | 
| Geekbench 6 CPU Single | 2385 | 3402 | 2348 | 2769 | 2137 | 
| Geekbench 6 CPU Multi | 6187 | 8508 | 9421 | 10930 | 9728 | 
| Geekbench 6 GPU (OpenCL) | 6019 | 19798 | 9554 | 28556 | 9689 | 
| Premiere 4K Export (lower is better) | 1 hour, 9 minutes, 29 seconds | 8 minutes, 30 seconds | Crashed | 7 minutes, 28 seconds | 12 minutes, 59 seconds | 
| Sustained SSD reads (MB/s) | 2394.57 | 1735.91 | 3804.31 | 6391.51 | 5738.86 | 
| Sustained SSD writes (MB/s) | 2092.66 | 1684.05 | 3310.94 | 5524.22 | 2801.02 | 
| Price as tested | $449 | $699 | $949.99 | $1,049.99 | $749.99 | 
But despite faster storage, the UniBook’s 8GB of RAM is still a hindrance on Windows 11. It didn’t randomly lag like the recent 13-inch Surface Laptop did, but it isn’t hard to overwhelm. As on the 8GB Surface, Windows 11 uses anywhere from 4.6 to over 5GB of memory on the UniBook after a fresh reboot with no additional apps running. Once you open a half dozen Chrome tabs, a couple messaging apps, and a music streaming app, memory usage easily climbs to 7GB.
It’s no surprise Chrome crashed on me a couple times when I pushed it further with over 20 tabs across multiple virtual desktops. This is no problem on Windows laptops with 16GB of RAM, and even the MacBook Neo could handle more before slowing down. And you can count on everything moving like molasses during big file transfers. It couldn’t even load the Start menu or open the calculator app while importing photos into Lightroom Classic until the RAM and SSD bottlenecks eased.
Even if your computing needs are minimal, the Chuwi’s hardware makes every interaction unpleasant. The screen is washed out, covering just 64 percent of the sRGB color space, and at 300 nits it’s pretty dim. But the worst offender is the trackpad. It’s incredibly stiff to click. You have to press it so hard the whole chassis flexes a little under the pressure. You don’t have to click the trackpad; it can detect taps too, but I never like the loosey-goosey feel of tapping — especially when executing right-clicks or click-and-drags. Using this trackpad made me physically and mentally tired. And clicking around on a laptop? Pretty important!
The speakers are an affront to any music you play, as well as anyone else within earshot. They’re a tinny mess. The phone in your pocket has fuller sound. The 720p webcam is only a smidge better, but it’s still offensive to your face (and possibly your self-confidence). It’s almost passable in the best lighting, but it’s low-res, with a green color cast. In dim or backlit lighting you become a dark blur. After a few days, colleagues started greeting me in meetings with, “Oh, you must be on the Chuwi.” It’s like being told “Wow, you look tired.”
“Uhh, yeah. Nice to see you too.”
Amid all these downsides, there are a few bright spots. The UniBook does at least have good battery life. It easily lasts up to 10 hours on battery while doing the lightest of work: writing emails, casually browsing the web, and opening the occasional PDF. And the keyboard isn’t bad. It’s backlit, which is a genuine advantage over the MacBook Neo. It’s fine to type on, but the Neo’s and many other Windows keyboards out there feel less spongy. Also, a lack of function lock means adjusting brightness, volume, or media playback always requires a two-key combo. Not a huge deal, but a strange omission of a usual mainstay.
The one thing about the UniBook that genuinely surprised me, aside from the initial reverse sticker shock, was its amount of ports. This little thing has five total USB ports, HDMI-out, microSD, and even an ethernet jack. You might expect all that on a massive gaming laptop, not a thin-and-light. But sadly, none of the USBs are faster than 5Gbps, and the HDMI is just 1.4b — topping out at a stuttery 30Hz at 4K.
Any money spent on peripherals to offset the Chuwi’s shortcomings would be better spent on a different laptop. I’ve started testing a $500-ish HP OmniBook 3, and coming from the Chuwi, it was a huge relief. Even its cheap-as-they-get Snapdragon X chip offers eight cores, buoyed by twice the RAM and storage of the Chuwi, and that processor already proved it had exceptional battery life when I reviewed it in the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3x.
I wasn’t overly impressed with the Acer Aspire 14 AI, which you can often get around $600, when I pitted it and the IdeaPad against the MacBook Neo, but it’s way better than the Chuwi for $155 more. Its Intel Lunar Lake chip gets good battery life and is powerful enough to play indie games and last-gen 3D titles on ultra-low settings. It has twice the RAM and storage as the Chuwi and nearly as many ports, and the Acer’s ports are much faster.
I take no joy in telling you the Chuwi UniBook is bad and frustrating to use. I want to see decent cheap laptops, and I’m all for them coming from lesser-known brands. But Chuwi’s upstart status also brings long-term customer support into question — it doesn’t seem to have US customer service and repair centers like bigger laptop makers. And in early 2026, the company was found to have shipped laptops and mini PCs with older AMD chips disguised as newer, faster ones (even at the BIOS level). Chuwi eventually put out a statement blaming a “production error” and offered refunds for a limited time, but the situation does not inspire confidence.
The UniBook doesn’t leave a great first impression, but I want to remain hopeful that better things are on the horizon — if not for Chuwi, then at least for the Wildcat Lake processor family. Most of the major laptop makers are launching budget laptops with higher-end Wildcat Lake chips to try to compete with the Neo. Microsoft also claims it’s working on improving Windows 11’s performance with 8GB of RAM — which these new laptops desperately need.
With laptop prices skyrocketing due to the RAM and storage crunch, we could all use a win. But the UniBook isn’t it.
Chuwi UniBook specs (as reviewed)
- Display: 14-inch 1920 x 1200 60Hz IPS LCD, 300 nits, anti-glare
- CPU: Intel Core 3 304 (Wildcat Lake, 5 cores)
- GPU: Integrated Intel Graphics
- RAM: 8GB LPDDR5 (soldered)
- Storage: 256GB M.2 2280 (user-accessible)
- Webcam: 720p with physical privacy shutter
- Connectivity: Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.2
- Ports: 2x USB-C 3.2 Gen 1 (5Gbps), 2x USB-A 3.2 Gen 1 (5Gbps), 1x USB-A 2.0 (480Mbps), HDMI 1.4b, RJ-45 gigabit ethernet, microSD card slot, 3.5mm audio jack
- Biometrics: none (lockscreen password only)
- Weight: 2.66 pounds / 1.2kg
- Dimensions: 12.38 x 8.7 x 0.65 inches / 314.5 x 221 x 16.4mm
- Battery: 53.38Wh (65W USB-C charger included)
- Price: $449
Photography by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

articles.title: Giá xăng dầu hôm nay 8/8: Thế giới tăng nhẹ, trong nước duy trì mức thấp
articles.text:
Giá dầu thế giới hôm nay
Giá dầu quốc tế trong phiên giao dịch cuối cùng của tuần này (7/8) tăng nhẹ.
Kết thúc phiên giao dịch 7/8, theo dữ liệu từ Oilprice, giá dầu Brent niêm yết ở mức 83,55 USD/thùng, tăng 1,29% so với phiên liền trước. Còn giá dầu WTI chốt phiên ở mức 78,18 USD/thùng, tăng 1,15%.
Giá dầu thế giới tiếp tục đi lên vào phiên cuối tuần khi giới đầu tư lo ngại về kết quả của các cuộc đàm phán liên quan đến việc kiểm soát và mở cửa trở lại eo biển Hormuz. Đây là tuyến hàng hải quan trọng, vận chuyển khoảng 1/5 lượng dầu mỏ và khí đốt tự nhiên hóa lỏng của toàn thế giới trước khi chiến sự giữa Mỹ và Iran bắt đầu vào cuối tháng Hai.
Trong phiên giao dịch 6/8, giá dầu Brent tới tăng 3,83% sau khi Iran xem xét dự luật cấm tàu Mỹ và Israel đi qua eo biển Hormuz.
Các chuyên gia cho rằng những tín hiệu về khả năng đạt được thỏa thuận về việc kiểm soát và mở cửa trở lại eo biển Hormuz trong tuần này khiến tâm lý thị trường biến động mạnh. Song giới đầu tư vẫn chưa rõ cần những điều kiện nào để các bên tiến tới một thỏa thuận chính thức.
Iran và Oman được cho là đã thống nhất tuyến đường dành cho các tàu đi qua eo biển nằm giữa hai nước. Nhưng khả năng Mỹ chấp thuận các điều khoản trên vẫn còn bỏ ngỏ.
Một quan chức cấp cao của Iran cho hay nước này đang yêu cầu mức phí từ 5-7% giá trị hàng hóa vận chuyển qua eo biển. Trong khi đó, Oman đang thảo luận về mức phí khoảng 3%, còn Washington thì không muốn thu bất kỳ khoản phí nào.
Các nhà phân tích cũng nhận định rằng những diễn biến trong tuần này cho thấy xung đột giữa Iran và Mỹ vẫn chưa thực sự chấm dứt.
Giá xăng dầu trong nước hôm nay
Giá bán các mặt hàng xăng dầu phổ biến tại thị trường trong nước vào hôm nay (8/8) được áp dụng như sau:
Theo kỳ điều hành ngày 6/8, giá xăng E10 giảm 535 đồng/lít, giá bán không cao hơn 22.324 đồng/lít. Giá xăng E5 giảm 660 đồng/lít, giá bán không cao hơn 21.728 đồng/lít.
Tương tự, giá dầu diesel giảm 80 đồng/lít, giá bán không cao hơn 27.544 đồng/lít.
Còn giá dầu mazut giảm 87 đồng/kg, giá bán không cao hơn 16.391 đồng/kg.
Liên quan đến thị trường xăng dầu, chỉ trong 7 tháng đầu năm, nước ta đã chi ra 12,31 tỷ USD để nhập khẩu 13,65 triệu tấn dầu thô và xăng dầu các loại.
Hiện giá xăng dầu ở nước ta được điều chỉnh sát với diễn biến giá thế giới. Số liệu cập nhật đến ngày 6/8 của Bộ Công Thương cho thấy, giá xăng dầu bán lẻ tại Việt Nam thuộc nhóm thấp nhất trong khu vực.
Cụ thể, đối với xăng, giá bán lẻ tại Việt Nam ở mức 22.324 đồng/lít. Trong khi ở Thái Lan xăng có giá 28.750 đồng/lít, Campuchia là 28.838 đồng/lít, Trung Quốc 32.383 đồng/lít và Lào ở mức 44.916 đồng/lít.
Với mặt hàng dầu diesel, giá bán lẻ tại Việt Nam là 27.544 đồng/lít, còn ở Thái Lan là 28.750 đồng/lít, Trung Quốc 29.366 đồng/lít, Campuchia 33.698 đồng/lít và Lào 37.548 đồng/lít.

articles.title: Spokane Shows What the New Era of Wildfires Looks Like
articles.text:
Betsy Robertson was standing in the center of the Spokane Convention Center on Monday afternoon, but she wasn’t there for a gala or a conference. Instead, the event space in the middle of Washington state’s second-largest city had been transformed into a Red Cross emergency shelter as a trio of wildfires, just a few miles away, burned down entire neighborhoods.
Nurses and volunteers were moving between the rows of cots around Robertson, making sure that the hundreds of evacuees—from the mothers with their babies to the elderly with their caretakers—had blankets and enough to eat. Just outside, the air was noxious with smoke “thick enough to burn your eyes,” she said.
Robertson, a communications director for the Red Cross, is from Washington and has been with the organization for 10 years. She has seen communities devastated by wildfires before. But never like this.
“The scale of homes destroyed and lives changed forever—this is a new level,” she said. “We are bracing ourselves for seasons like this getting worse and worse, and starting earlier and going later.”
A historically dry winter, extreme drought, and heat waves set the stage for the hundreds of wildfires that have burned across the Pacific Northwest this summer. Dozens of large ones have broken out in the past week alone. Though it’s still early in the fire season, Oregon recently broke its annual record for acreage burned with nearly 2 million acres scorched.
Washington is also in the middle of its most destructive season on record, with more than half a million acres burned and at least 65,000 residents ordered to evacuate across the state. The three large fires that started on Saturday around Spokane had destroyed more than 700 buildings by Monday afternoon.
“I’ve been trying to wrap my mind around how we’re going to house all these folks,” said Kitty Klitzke, a member of the Spokane City Council representing a hard-hit area where two fires were burning on Tuesday morning. Many of the people displaced by the fires in Spokane are senior citizens and their caretakers. “It’s a miracle that, so far, we know of no fatalities and no reported missing people,” Klitzke said.
As the planet heats up, the conditions that fuel extreme wildfires are becoming more common. A warmer atmosphere can hold about 7 percent more water vapor for every 1 degree Celsius of warming, drawing more moisture from soils and vegetation and leaving forests and grasslands primed to burn. That dynamic also causes rain to fall more intensely but less frequently, leading to long periods of drought.
“This fire, and what we’re expecting to come, makes no sense unless you connect the dots through a changing climate,” said Bob Freitag, who recently served as director of the Institute of Hazards Mitigation Research and Planning at the University of Washington. “The science is known, and this is not something that is a one-off.”
According to Paul Pastelok, a senior meteorologist at AccuWeather, a lack of snowfall across the region helped set the stage for these fires. Normally, snowpack builds up during the winter and melts gradually through the rest of the year, providing a steady source of moisture. This year, the already-small snowpack was hit with hot spring temperatures, causing this reserve to melt early and leaving the landscape parched. Spokane had half of the typical snowfall this year, Pastelok said. Other parts of the state had even less, with many areas reaching historic lows.
In the past few days, powerful winds carried hot embers from the Little Giant fire, a 70,000-acre blaze in central Washington, for more than 3 miles, sending the flames clear over the waters of Lake Chelan and into the forests on the other side. Ryan Rodruck, a communications manager at the Washington Department of Natural Resources, called the overall situation “extremely tragic” and said that it had been an exceptionally challenging season for the thousands of wildland firefighters deployed across the state.
In Spokane, more high winds forecast for this weekend could further worsen conditions, said Benjamin Cossel, a wildfire public information officer from California working with firefighting crews in the city.
The situation is comparable to the Los Angeles fires in 2025, Cossel said. Both outbreaks began in wild areas before moving into partially forested suburban neighborhoods. The urban setting also makes the smoke especially toxic, he said. A recently released study found that the Los Angeles fires, which sent more than 200,000 residents fleeing, had exposed an estimated 3.3 million people to high concentrations of a cancer-causing toxin.
Klitzke, the city council member, said the affected neighborhoods in Spokane were known to be vulnerable to fires. Steep terrain and abundant plant life helped the fires spread quickly over the weekend, while the winding cul-de-sac layouts of the neighborhoods slowed evacuations and made it difficult for emergency responders to reach the fires.
“These are neighborhoods with thousands of people and only two ways in or out,” Klitzke said, adding that many evacuees were stuck waiting in traffic for hours, watching the houses around them burn down.
Areas where homes mingle with natural areas are known as the wildland-urban interface. This kind of suburban housing is the fastest growing type of land development in the United States, and research shows that the homes built in these areas are more likely to burn down when wildfires spread.
“We already knew that this was a dangerous situation,” she said. “We need to get really serious about addressing climate change.”
Increasingly, fire-prone states like California are requiring homeowners to clear the trees and shrubs in a radius surrounding their home. This buffer zone, known as a defensible space, can dramatically reduce the risk that a wildfire will ignite a building.
People chose to live in these neighborhoods precisely because they love the vegetation, Cossel said. “I understand why people don’t want to remove them,” he said. “But we can’t live in that world anymore because of these fires.”
This story was originally published by Grist and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

articles.title: My favorite feel-good show is back
articles.text:
Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 139, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, barbecue sauce, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)
My favorite feel-good show is back
Plus, in this week’s Installer: A new all-purpose backpack, the latest Bose cans, an Anthony Bourdain movie, and more.
This week, I’ve been reading about Johnny Knoxville and Google Zero and the history of the bicycle, @all-ing everyone in all my WhatsApp chats just because I can now, rereading There Will Come Soft Rains because this week is when it happens, seeing if Sabbath can help fix my screentime problems, once again moving everything around in my home office, eating altogether too much of the fabulous Trader Joe’s snack mix, testing the Clicks Power Keyboard, and starting to prep for my fantasy football drafts. Because I will not finish last again.
I also have for you the return of a favorite TV show, some new bags for toting all your gear, a couple of exciting new Android apps, and much more. Let’s go.
(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What are you watching / reading / playing / listening to / hacking into with your AI agent this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)
The Drop
- Ted Lasso season 4. Lots of good reviews for the new season, which is also kind of a soft reboot of the franchise. And all the bad ones are like, “why isn’t there any conflict, this show is too happy,” which I count as a good review anyway. Give me more shows that make me feel better at the end of every episode.
- The Peak Design City Backpack. The whole lineup of City products — which includes totes, crossbody bags, and more — looks great, but I’m a backpack guy at heart. Love a dedicated AirTag pocket, love an integrated hook, love the mix of clean design and tons of organization. I really don’t need a new backpack, and yet…
- Bose QuietComfort headphones. Noise-canceling headphones are like AI models, in that it seems every one’s the best until the next one comes out three days later. I’m excited about Bose’s adaptive EQ for dialogue and the improved passthrough when you want the ANC off. I also like the mint color. A lot.
- Nothing’s CMF Clip Pro. More headphones! Nothing’s buds are generally hard to beat for $100. Also, open earbuds are awesome. Throw in the awesome orange color I already love in my Shokz headphones, and I’m getting alarmingly close to two headphone purchases this week.
- Tony. After BlackBerry, director Matt Johnson is officially in my “I will watch anything he does” category of filmmakers. Johnson’s latest, a story about how Anthony Bourdain got his start as a chef, has gotten good reviews and is very much at the intersection of all my interests.
- Sunbird. “iMessage for Android” is one of those ideas that just won’t quit, and now Sunbird is back with big promises about fixing its previous security issues. You should always tread super carefully with these messaging aggregators, but they really are a useful idea.
- Notability for Android. FINALLY. After months of promises and more months of beta tests, one of the most powerful note-taking apps is officially shipping to Android devices everywhere. I haven’t used it a ton, but so far it’s stable and fast — it’s a particularly big win if you’re the handwriting type.
- The Sega Dreamcast Watch. From Sega and SuperGroupies comes an extremely rad series of watches designed like old consoles. You can also get the Mega Drive and the Sega Saturn models, but for me there’s no beating the color pop of the Dreamcast’s controls.
JA Westenberg is one of those people who always seems to be blogging about what I’m thinking about. “I Deleted My Second Brain” still rattles around my head whenever I’m needlessly fiddling with a note-taking app, I used the word “cockroachmaxxing” unironically in conversation the other day, and I’m forever jealous of the insight that YouTube “looks increasingly like a single show with five million hosts.”
They’ve also built a couple of really cool productivity-adjacent apps, including Kerouac (which is basically like that GitHub commit chart but for writing) and recently Post Through It, which is basically a journaling app that looks like a private Twitter. Clever!
Anyway, I asked JA to share their homescreen to see if they might have other sneaky tips up their sleeve, or more awesome apps to show. Here it is, plus some info on the apps they use and why:
The phone: I use an iPhone 17 Pro Max, 512GB.
The wallpaper: My wallpaper is Mors Imperator (“Death Is the Ruler”), by the German artist Hermione von Preuschen. It’s on display in Berlin right now and I fell in love with it on a recent trip. She was famously banned from displaying it, and instead rented a house and charged an entry fee to see it. Very punk rock / DIY for the 1800s.
The apps: Insight Timer, Beeper, Spotify, Pocket Casts, Buffer, Cursor, 1Password, Replit, Termius, Granola, Kilo, Kerouac, Post Through It, Buzz, Wikipedia, Marvel Unlimited, Linear, Medium, GenZD, The New York Times, Obsidian, Vimcal, Readwise Reader, Kobo.
My home screen is a mix of reading, working, playing etc. I definitely want to call out Kerouac (a writing studio for pro bloggers) and Post Through It (microblogging for one) which are PWAs of the apps I launched this year. I’m a big believer in web apps as a way to avoid app store gatekeeping, so I’m on a mission to make the PWAs of my own tools as top-notch as they can be, which means using them every day myself.
I keep the Kobo app in my dock so I push myself to read an actual book instead of doomscrolling; and I don’t keep any social media apps installed. If I want to post, I have Buffer on my home screen, and it’s connected to my Hermes agent via MCP anyway. I use Beeper to manage my chats across Discord, Slack, Telegram, Signal, WhatsApp, etc; it’s a fantastic tool that probably rescues me from chat hell a thousand times a day.
GenZD and Marvel Unlimited are my favorites. The first is a GZDoom client for playing Doom 1 and Doom 2, Heretic, Hexen, and their mods (3D shooters from the ’90s). The other is Marvel’s digital comics app, where I’m attempting to read every Spider-Man story since the inception of the character. Other than that, it’s work, note-taking and podcasts.
I also asked JA to share a few things they’re into right now. Here’s what they sent back:
- I have rediscovered my love for MC Lars. He’s a “nerdcore” indie rapper who came to fame with songs about Edgar Allan Poe, Shakespeare etc. He’s been a favorite of mine for years, but I introduced my kid to his music this year, and he’s been in constant rotation since. “I Was Never Afraid” is his all time best song.
- The Paradox are the best band I’ve heard in a decade. They play pop punk the way it should be played, with so much energy and joy I can’t not jump out of my seat when I hear it. I recommend their track “Good For Me,” which I think is going to be on their new EP in October.
- I’ve been reading Barbarians at the Gate: the Fall of RJR Nabisco, by Bryan Burrough and John Helyar. A wild story of leveraged buyouts, Wall Street excess, and the unhinged market economics of the 1980s. An absolute page turner, even if you’re not usually interested in the subject matter.
- My brother has started us on a Daggerheart campaign. It’s a tabletop RPG that came out last year, with a heavy emphasis on storytelling, and it’s the freshest take on roleplaying I’ve experienced in a while. Really makes you want to get inside the character you’re running and think about who they are — which is a great exercise for me as a writer.
Crowdsourced
Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Threads and this post on Bluesky.
“Madden NFL 27 Mobile came out! The wild part? The Apple Arcade version removes **ALL** of the recent enshittification: ads, virtual currencies, paywalls, etc. Add in the controller and Apple TV support, and it feels like playing Madden from the early 2000s, in the best way.” — Brian
“I’m waiting for my Retroid Pocket Nova so I can replay Rogue Squadron on GameCube and Need for Speed: Carbon on PS2, and I’m organizing my ROM library before it arrives.” — Josue
“Moved my gaming PC to CachyOS (tried Bazzite before and got a little frustrated). So far it’s been amazing. Also, I just upgraded my PC case from an old NZXT one to a Fractal North. These cases are no joke. So well made.” — Kolin
“Silo season three.” — Amanda
“Biological War: A Scenario from Annie Jacobsen, the author of Nuclear War: A Scenario. I honestly cannot believe it’s that easy to wipe us off the planet.” — Dawit
“Found this neat little Mac OS app, Hoy, for communicating via iCloud. Quite digging the simple UI and how it ‘sits’ nicely inside my menu bar.” — Julius
“Reading John Ousterhout’s excellent A Philosophy of Software Design to get ready for a presentation I’m making at the gRPC conference next month.” — Tim
“Watching the anime Jaadugar: A Witch in Mongolia. I’m enjoying learning about that period of history (the show took me into a Wikipedia hole), and I’m excited to see how the magic elements come into play.” — J
Signing off
I’m about to go on parental leave, which previously in my life has been a good time to change stuff on my phone. I delete all the work apps, turn off some notifications, all that stuff. But you know what’s really making me do it this time? The Google Health app. I haven’t been wearing my Fitbit Air recently — no good reason, just haven’t been finding it useful — and every single day the app sends me a sad notification that’s like, “Oh no, I haven’t collected any data, pretty please let’s get the Fitbit back on?” No thanks, I hate it.
Anyway, I’ve also been noticing that some of the smartest people I know are always showing that they “have notifications silenced” in iMessage. So I’m learning from them, and turning everything off. From now on, my phone will have no buzzing or noise-making notifications other than phone calls. I’ll see things when I decide to check my phone… which hopefully won’t be very often. Silent phones forever!
In theory, I’m here next week before I head out. If not, you’ll be in the very capable hands of Jay Peters for a while. Either way, see you next week!

articles.title: Supernatural's head of fitness on rebooting the VR exercise app after leaving Meta - Engadget
articles.text:
Supernatural's head of fitness on rebooting the VR exercise app after leaving Meta
Leanne Pedante discusses why she’s excited about this next phase of Supernatural.
It's rare for tech companies to get a second chance at life, but that's the story of the VR exercise platform Supernatural. After Meta announced that it was cutting the company's staff and pausing new content for the exercise app in January Supernatural made the surprising revelation that it will be relaunching later this year as an independent company. While it's getting a bit more expensive — back to its original launch pricing of $20 a month or $200 a year — that probably won't deter the company's superfans, many of whom were heartbroken about the app's potential shutdown.
So what's next for Supernatural? Leanne Pedante, one of Supernatural's founding coaches and its current Head of Fitness, says the company is currently working on bringing back everything its existing users love with its reboot. "We have a library of over 3,000 workouts that we've built over the years — all of that comes back," she said in an interview on the Engadget Podcast. "The same coaches, the same beautiful environments. We're working on our music negotiations right now. We'll also start releasing new content, which hasn't been happening for quite a while now."
Based on her conversations with Supernatural's community, Pedante says many members are onboard with the new plan, even given the price hikes. (Members of the Supernatural subreddit aren't as pleased.) New and existing subscribers can sign up to be Founding Members of the new app for a slightly discounted $180 subscription for the first year.
"The other thing that's been really cool is that because we're a small team now... essentially we're a flat organization," she added. "There's no bureaucracy. We can move really fast. And so immediately we were able to respond to people talking about there being a [paywall] barrier by creating a Supernatural scholarship program."
In its FAQ, the company says that limited scholarships will be offered quarterly to members undergoing financial hardships. They'll be reviewed by Supernatural's team to "grant support where it's needed most." Some members have also suggested that they'd want to pay for someone else's membership.
Even with a slight price increase, Supernatural's cost and convenience is still well below a typical fitness club, or even community clubs like the YMCA. There's no need to commute to another place, no traces of other people's sweat on equipment and none of the horrors of the communal showers. Of course, that also means you don't get the benefits of exercise facilities, which typically offer a variety of equipment for more intense workouts. You won't get much cardio or strength work done with just a headset alone. And of course, you'll also have to shell out $350 for the Meta Quest 3S or a whopping $600 for the Quest 3, both of which are far more expensive than they were at launch.
Similar to VRChat, Supernatural has also built up a core group of users who love the community building aspects of the app. She recently spent two weekends at meetups in Seattle and Denver, where she was able to chat with hundreds of subscribers, including a couple that got married after working out together in Supernatural.
While VR is at the core of Supernatural — its Chris Milk and Aaron Koblin founded the app as part of their VR studio Within — there's potential for its workouts to reach even more people with devices like the Nex Playground. It uses a camera to capture what you're doing and project digital objects on your TV; similar to Microsoft's Kinect, it can support games that are controller- and headset-free.
"I can definitely say that we're actively exploring where else to meet our members outside of headsets," Pedante said. "I think in fitness for sure, one of the main things that allows a person to create consistency and create a habit is if you build trust and a relationship with your fitness community. And so once you've established that trust, which Supernatural members have established over the past six years with us and with each other, then, you want to be with those people to further your experience, right? So whether that's running, or a couch to 5K type of thing [training programs outside of headsets for members], people are absolutely interested in that, and we're exploring all of that."

articles.title: WhatsApp Gets a Handy @all Feature for Group Chats
articles.text:
The group chat is the last truly heavyweight institution of modern life. It’s one of the most reliable means of daily communication, used for just about anything from planning to catching up.
WhatsApp is counting over 3 billion users, and it’s a fair bet most of them are in at least one group chat; the platform has supported groups of up to 1,024 members since 2022.
An update that began rolling out on August 4 follows a run of group-focused releases earlier this year, including group message history, member tags, and event reminders. Taken together, it’s a clear signal of WhatsApp’s reliance on group chats as one of its defining features.
The platform’s latest update is designed to improve its usage, and it’s rolling out gradually. Here’s everything you need to know.
@all
Typing @all allows every member of the group to be notified, even the ones who muted the chat years ago. @all is designed to punch through and override the mute settings and notification preferences you set at chat level.
WhatsApp pitches this as a tool for the urgent stuff, like updates, changes, and last-minute cancellations. It has, however, also clearly anticipated the feature’s spam potential.
The spam safeguards thus work on two levels. In groups larger than 32 people, only admins can trigger @all, and the override itself has an off switch. You can also manually mute @all alerts entirely in your notification settings, a separate control from muting the chat itself. The 32-person threshold is the same cap WhatsApp applies to group calls. It’s the platform’s rough dividing line between a chat and a broadcast channel.
Polls
WhatsApp’s polling feature has been around since 2022 and is end-to-end encrypted like everything else on the platform. It is also, though, where many a group chat goes to stall. The poll fixes in the latest update are pragmatic.
You can now set an end time that automatically locks voting when it expires, giving the group a hard deadline to vote. Interestingly, you also have the option to hide voter names. Until now, WhatsApp polls were transparent by design, and everyone could see exactly who voted for what. Anonymizing votes now also exist inside an end-to-end encrypted system, where the whole architecture is built around verifying who sent what.
And you can now also edit a poll question within 15 minutes of posting it, which is the same grace window WhatsApp gives you to edit a regular message. Revolutionary stuff for the poll fiends among us.
Create Group Chats From Existing Groups
WhatsApp is formalizing the splinter chat. You can now whip up a new group chat from an existing one in a single tap, pulling members into a smaller group chat without having to manually add them one by one. The official use cases are surprises and side conversations that would otherwise clutter the main chat.
Usernames Are Coming
Away from group chats, WhatsApp also recently announced that usernames will launch later this year, allowing people to connect without sharing their phone numbers. The optional feature is designed as an added layer of privacy: Usernames can be changed or removed at any time and do not need to match your identity on another platform.
Reservations began rolling out in June, with eligible users able to claim a new name—or transfer an existing Facebook or Instagram handle—under the Account section in Settings. Users will also be able to add on a unique four-digit key before allowing someone can contact them.
WhatsApp says names associated with celebrities, public figures, and government bodies, including convincing imitations, will be reserved for their legitimate owners. The username land grab has officially begun.
This story was originally published by WIRED Middle East.
